questions.stem: A line of best fit passes through the points (4, 66) and (10, 96). Compute the slope of this line.
questions.explanation: Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x, so (96 minus 66) divided by (10 minus 4) equals 30 divided by 6, which is 5. This value means y rises by 5 units for each one-unit increase in x along the fitted line.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which variable in a bivariate study is the explanatory variable
questions.stem: A nutritionist records how many grams of protein each of 15 swimmers eats before practice and how long each swimmer rests afterward. Which variable is best treated as the explanatory variable?

options.misconception: Confuses mutual statistical relationship with interchangeable axis roles

options.text: Rest time, since it is the outcome that is expected to respond to the protein
options.misconception: Treats the response variable as the explanatory variable

options.text: Neither one, since a scatterplot always treats the two variables as equals
options.misconception: Believes axis choice prevents naming an explanatory variable

options.text: Grams of protein eaten, since it is the value the nutritionist recorded first

questions.explanation: The explanatory variable is the one whose values are set or recorded and then used to account for the other variable, which here is the protein amount. Rest time is the response because it is the measurement being explained.

options.misconception: Assumes a one-directional trend must be a straight-line trend

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the y-intercept of a line of best fit in context
questions.stem: For the fitted line score equals 55 plus 1.2 times hours, the intercept 55 is the predicted score when hours equals zero. Why must that reading be treated with care?

options.text: Because the intercept changes every time a new point is added to the graph
options.misconception: Believes the intercept of a fitted line is recomputed for each point

options.text: Because the intercept is a slope value that was accidentally divided by the wrong unit
options.misconception: Treats the intercept as a mis-scaled slope rather than a starting value

options.text: Because zero hours may lie far outside the hours that were actually observed
Because the intercept is the score of the single best student in the data set

questions.explanation: The intercept is the predicted value at an input of zero, and its meaning is only trustworthy if zero lies inside or near the range of the observed inputs. questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the error of predicting at an input far outside the observed range

options.misconception: Substitutes an unrelated variable for the one displayed on the axis

options.text: The prediction is perfectly reliable, since a fitted line holds for every value of x
options.misconception: Assumes the pattern of a fitted line extends without limit beyond the data

options.text: The prediction is wrong because a line of best fit cannot be used with values above 10 at all

questions.learningObjective: Compute the slope of a line through two points read from a graph
questions.stem: A line of best fit passes through the points (5, 70) and (15, 110). Compute the slope of this line.
questions.explanation: Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x, so (110 minus 70) divided by (15 minus 5) equals 40 divided by 10, which is 4. This means the line rises by 4 units of y for each one-unit increase in x.

options.text: The average percent of battery lost for each additional hour the device runs
The total battery percent lost over the whole run recorded in the data

options.text: The number of devices tested when the fitted line was constructed
options.misconception: Reads the slope as a count of observations in the sample

questions.hint: The coefficient of x is always a rate of change per unit of x.

questions.explanation: The predicted value at x equals 3 is 4 times 3 plus 18, which equals 30, and the observed value is 28. Subtracting gives 28 minus 30 equals -2, so the point lies 2 units below the fitted line.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the sign of a residual as indicating the side of the fitted line
questions.stem: For one observation the fitted line predicts 45 and the observed value is 50. Which statement about the residual and the position of the point is true?

options.text: The residual is 95, because the two values must be added together instead
options.misconception: Adds the observed and predicted values instead of subtracting them

options.text: The residual is negative 5, so the point sits below the fitted line
options.misconception: Subtracts in the reverse order and reverses the sign of the residual

options.text: The residual is positive 5, so the point sits above the fitted line
The residual is zero, because the point lies on the fitted line anyway
options.misconception: Assumes any point on a scatterplot lies on the fitted line

questions.explanation: A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value, so 50 minus 45 equals 5. A positive residual means the observation sits above the line at that x-value, because the measurement exceeded what the model anticipated.

options.misconception: Believes the sign of a residual carries no information about the side

options.text: The definition is reversed, but the final sign happens to be correct in this case
options.misconception: Believes reversing the subtraction leaves the sign unchanged

options.text: The student should have measured the horizontal gap between the point and the line
options.misconception: Measures the gap along the x-axis instead of the vertical gap

options.text: The definition is reversed, so the residual should be negative 3, not positive 3

questions.explanation: The standard definition is the observed value minus the predicted value, so a point above the line always produces a positive residual. Reversing the subtraction flips the sign, which means the student's reported value contradicts their own description of where the point lies.
questions.hint: Check whether the reported sign matches the side of the line the student described.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the error of reading a residual plot as a sign that the line is wrong
questions.stem: A residual plot for a fitted line shows points scattered randomly above and below zero, with no widening, curvature, or trend. A student says this pattern proves the fitted line is incorrect. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: The conclusion is correct, because residuals should all be exactly zero in a valid plot
options.misconception: Believes a valid residual plot must show every residual at zero

options.text: Random scatter around zero is the pattern a good linear fit is expected to produce
The conclusion is correct, because any vertical spread means the data are unrelated
options.misconception: Confuses scatter of residuals with an absence of association

options.text: The residual plot is not informative, because it cannot be read without a calculator
options.misconception: Treats residual plots as unreadable without computational tools

questions.explanation: A residual plot is a diagnostic: when the residuals fall randomly around zero with no systematic shape, the line has captured the linear pattern and only ordinary variation is left. Structure such as curvature, a widening fan, or a trend in the residuals is what signals an inadequate model.
questions.hint: Ask what pattern in a residual plot would indicate a problem with the line.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain how residual sum of squares compares the fit of two lines
questions.stem: Two candidate lines are fitted to the same 30 observations, and one produces a larger residual sum of squares than the other. Which line does the least squares criterion favor, and why?

options.text: Neither one, because residual sum of squares cannot be compared across two different lines
options.misconception: Claims the comparison statistic is incomparable between lines

options.text: The line with the larger residual sum of squares, because large misses carry more weight
options.misconception: Believes the criterion rewards the line with the biggest misses

options.text: The line with the smaller residual sum of squares, because that criterion rewards smaller misses
The line with more positive residuals than negative ones, since the signs cancel out
options.misconception: Believes the count of positive residuals decides the better line

questions.explanation: The least squares line is defined as the one that minimizes the total of the squared residuals, so a smaller residual sum of squares always indicates the preferred fit under that criterion. Comparing the sums directly avoids depending on the signs of individual residuals.
questions.hint: Recall what quantity the least squares line is chosen to make as small as possible.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the error of averaging residuals to judge a fit
questions.stem: A least squares line fitted to a scatterplot has residuals of positive 12, negative 3, positive 7, negative 4, and positive 2. A student claims that because they average to about 2.8 the line is fine with no further checking. What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: The reasoning is wrong because residuals cannot be averaged at all under any scheme
options.misconception: Claims residuals are not numeric values and so cannot be averaged

options.text: The reasoning is correct, because any positive average proves that the residuals sum to zero
options.misconception: Believes a nonzero average is the same thing as a zero sum of residuals

options.text: The reasoning is wrong because a least squares line must have residuals that are all positive
options.misconception: Assumes least squares fitting forces every residual to be positive

options.text: The average hides the wide spread of the individual misses, which must be examined separately

questions.explanation: A least squares line balances the residuals so their sum is zero, and the remaining question is how large the individual misses are. A single average figure cannot show whether the misses are tight or whether one observation misses badly, which is why the residual spread has to be inspected.
questions.hint: Ask whether one summary number can describe how far each point sits from the line.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a residual plot with curvature as evidence of a nonlinear relationship

options.text: The pattern means the residuals sum to zero, so the straight line is confirmed as adequate
options.misconception: Treats a balanced arrangement of residuals as confirmation of a good fit

options.text: The residuals show a systematic pattern, so a straight line is not capturing the true relationship
The pattern means the sample size is too small to draw any conclusion about the fit

options.text: The pattern means the axes were swapped, so the residual plot should be redrawn
options.misconception: Blames an axis reversal for structure that reflects a nonlinear trend

questions.explanation: A curved run through a residual plot is a systematic miss, meaning the straight line predicts too high at one end and too low at the other. That structure means the relationship is not linear, so a different functional form should be considered for the fit.
questions.hint: A good fit leaves residuals randomly scattered, not arranged in a recognizable shape.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a correlation coefficient from a claim of cause and effect
questions.stem: A researcher finds a correlation coefficient of -0.91 between hours spent doing homework and hours spent watching television for 60 students. Which conclusion about cause and effect is supported?

options.text: Watching more television causes less homework, because the values move in opposite directions
options.misconception: Assumes a correlation proves the direction it happens to be stated in

options.text: Doing less homework causes more television watching, because the coefficient is strong and negative
options.misconception: Reads a strong negative correlation as a one-way causal relationship

options.text: Neither one is supported, because a correlation alone cannot establish which variable causes the other
A confounding factor such as sleep is impossible, because the correlation is so close to negative one
options.misconception: Believes a strong correlation rules out the influence of a third variable

questions.explanation: A correlation coefficient measures how tightly two variables move together in a straight-line pattern, and it carries no information about which variable drives the other. Even a coefficient near negative one can arise from a third variable that affects both, or from reversed causation, so no causal direction is established.
questions.hint: Ask what a correlation coefficient can measure and what it cannot.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a lurking variable can produce a correlation without causation
questions.stem: Cities with more fire trucks sent to a blaze also tend to report larger fire damage, and the correlation is strong. A reporter concludes that sending more trucks causes more damage and recommends sending fewer. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.misconception: Claims the response variable is unmeasurable rather than confounded

options.text: The reasoning is sound, because a strong correlation is enough to justify the recommendation
options.misconception: Treats the strength of a correlation as a sufficient basis for a decision

options.text: The reasoning is wrong only because the damage values were reported by different cities
options.misconception: Blames inconsistent reporting instead of recognizing a common cause

options.text: Fire size is a lurking variable that raises both the number of trucks sent and the damage reported

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an experiment rather than an observational study is needed to support causation
questions.stem: A nutritionist observes a strong positive correlation between protein intake and muscle gain in a group of volunteers and wants to claim that protein intake causes the gain. Which design would best support that claim?

options.text: A second observational survey that reproduces the same correlation in a new group
options.misconception: Thinks repeating the same observational design is equivalent to randomizing

options.text: A larger observational survey that measures intake and gain in more people
options.misconception: Assumes increasing the sample size converts an association into a cause

options.text: A scatterplot with a tighter cloud of points around the fitted line
options.misconception: Believes increasing the strength of an association establishes a cause

options.text: An experiment that randomly assigns volunteers to different protein intake levels

questions.explanation: A causal claim requires a design that manipulates the suspected cause while holding other factors balanced across groups, which is what random assignment provides. Observational studies, however large or well-replicated, cannot rule out alternative explanations for the association.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the strength and sign of a stated correlation coefficient

options.misconception: Converts a signed coefficient into a causal claim about direction

questions.explanation: A coefficient near zero indicates a weak linear relationship, while the positive sign says that larger values of one variable tend to go with larger values of the other. Neither the size nor the sign of the coefficient says anything about which variable influences the other.
questions.hint: Read the magnitude first, then the sign, and keep cause out of the reading.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a controlled experiment from an uncontrolled comparison of groups
questions.stem: A school compares test scores of students who chose to join a tutoring club with scores of students who did not, and finds the club members scored higher. Which feature most limits the claim that tutoring caused the higher scores?

options.text: The club met only once, so no tutoring effect could ever be detected at all
options.misconception: Assumes a single session rules out any measurable effect

options.text: The two groups had different sizes, since unequal samples always invalidate a comparison
options.misconception: Treats unequal group sizes as automatically fatal to any comparison

options.text: Test scores cannot be compared across students in the same school year
options.misconception: Claims identical populations cannot be compared on their scores

options.text: Students selected themselves into the groups, so motivation may differ before tutoring begins

questions.explanation: Because students chose whether to join the club, the groups may differ in motivation, prior grades, or other factors that affect scores. Without random assignment to balance those factors, the observed score gap cannot be attributed to tutoring itself.
questions.hint: Ask who decided which students were in each group.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a fitted line can be used for prediction without implying causation
questions.stem: A line of best fit predicts thunderstorm distance from the number of seconds counted between lightning and thunder. Which statement correctly separates prediction from causation here?

options.text: The line is useless for prediction, because a fitted line must always identify a cause
options.misconception: Believes prediction requires an established causal mechanism

options.text: The line predicts distance from the counted seconds without claiming that the count causes the distance
The line proves that counting more seconds moves a thunderstorm farther away
options.misconception: Treats a predictive relationship as a one-way causal mechanism

options.text: The line can only be used when the two quantities are measured in the same units
options.misconception: Assumes a fitted line requires matching units on both axes

questions.explanation: A line of best fit is a predictive summary of how two variables move together, and it works perfectly well as a calculator for new inputs. Using it to predict a distance from a counted time says nothing about which astronomical quantity is the cause of the other.
questions.hint: Separate what the line computes from what it claims about cause.
